narrow-band filter surveys can be used to detect large number densities of quasars with high precision in their photometrically derived redshifts and that this will enable the measurement of the baryon acoustic peak in the quasar correlation function up to z∽ 2–3.

a narrow-band optical imaging survey could detect quasar number densities as high or higher than the current state of the art, and that it could deliver photometric redshift accuracies as high or higher as those obtained with current spectroscopic surveys.
narrow-band filter surveys can measure the large-scale structure of the Universe with quasars at high redshift.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the potential use of quasars for cosmological purposes, and in particular, to measure large-scale structure.
the use of quasars as tracers of the large-scale structure, which can be done in a very efficient way with narrow-band filter surveys.
the potential of narrow-band surveys to measure large-scale structure with unprecedented precision.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
quasars are an excellent probe of large-scale structure and baryon acoustic fluctuations, and that narrow-band surveys are the best way to obtain them.
narrow-band filter surveys can be used to measure large-scale structure, and that the J-PAS is a good example of this type of surveys.

a narrow-band optical filter imaging survey, such as J-PAS, could provide a large number of quasars with accurate photometric redshift estimates, and therefore be used to study large-scale structure in the Universe.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
quasars are a very promising probe to measure the power spectrum of the large-scale structure up to redshifts of z∼ 2–3.
a narrow-band filter survey can provide a powerful tool to study the large-scale structure of the Universe, and that J-PAS is a good example of such a survey.

a large-area narrow-band filter survey, such as J-PAS, could be used to measure the power spectrum up z≃ 4, and to measure baryonic acoustic oscillations at z≳ 2.5, with a precision comparable to that of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a large-area narrow-band imaging survey can be an excellent tool to study the growth and the expansion of the Universe.

quasars can be turned into a very useful cosmological probe, and that the J-PAS survey will be able to provide the first high-accuracy measurements of the power-spectrum amplitude and the baryon acoustic scale at z∼1–2.

narrow-band surveys are a powerful and efficient tool to measure large-scale structure at high redshift, and they can be used in combination with spectroscopic follow-up to deliver the most precise measurements of the power-spectrum and baryon acoustic-oscillation peak.
